title: Syncing across devices
summary: Offline edits need durable local intent, a cursor and a plan for old devices.

steps.title: The note returns after you delete it
steps.text: You delete a note on your phone. A laptop has been offline for a month and later uploads its old copy. Without a record of the deletion, the server may treat that copy as new. Sync is a protocol for reconciling histories, not just downloading the current rows.

steps.title: Send changes, keep intent
steps.text: Save each local edit and a device outbox entry in one durable transaction before showing it as saved on this device. Give the operation a stable id, a device sequence and a base version. Upload retries use the same id. The server commits the operation and deduplication result together, then returns its version. An upload acknowledgement must not advance the pull cursor past other changes the device has never downloaded. Pull after the last committed pull cursor, then commit the downloaded changes and that cursor together locally. Opaque cursors may include an epoch so a rebuilt log cannot be mistaken for the old one. A lost cursor can trigger a snapshot tied to a log position, followed by deltas from that position. Preserve local unsynced edits separately during this rebase.

steps.title: Worked example: a day of edits
steps.text: A notebook has 10,000 notes averaging 2 KB. A full refresh downloads about 20 MB. If 50 notes changed today, a delta costs about 100 KB before metadata, about 200 times less. A timer scheduled every minute makes up to 1,440 polling attempts a day while allowed to run. The operating system may coalesce or suspend them; timer firings are not a measurement of radio wakeups. A push can say changes are ready so the client pulls authenticated deltas. Push is a wake-up hint, not the durable delivery channel. Sleeping phones and mobile operating systems may delay it. Under-a-second propagation is a foreground connected-device target; background delivery is eventual. The sim can show network traffic, but cannot measure radio wakeups or offline convergence.

rows.label: Minute polling attempts
rows.how: 24 × 60 if allowed to run; actual wakeups depend on the OS and radio

steps.q: A client persists its pull cursor before committing downloaded changes, then crashes. What can happen?
choices: The next pull repeats the changes because the server can see the crash
The next pull skips changes that never committed locally
The server deduplicates uploads, which also repairs the missing downloads
steps.why: The server cannot infer local application. Commit pulled changes and their cursor in one local transaction.

steps.q: Why is an on-device outbox necessary? Follow-up: the user closes the app just after an edit.
checklist: Commit the note and its upload intent in one local transaction
Say when saved locally becomes durably synced to the server
Resume the same operation id after app termination or reboot
steps.model: A network call after a local edit leaves a crash window. I would save the edit and its outbox operation together before confirming local save. On restart, the outbox resumes with the same id. The screen says saved on this device until the server durably accepts it. That does not protect against losing the device itself before syncing, and the product must make that distinction clear.

steps.title: Keep deletions and expose conflicts
steps.text: A tombstone says a particular identity was deleted at a version. Keep it until the supported offline horizon and replica recovery rules make forgetting safe. If clients may be offline for 30 days, a shorter tombstone lifetime risks resurrection. Devices returning beyond the horizon must rebase from a fresh snapshot. Validate the upload epoch or reject unknown base versions even after tombstones expire, so a missing old identity is not mistaken for a new note. Concurrent whole-note edits can become conflict copies. A text CRDT may preserve more intent but adds metadata, testing and encryption constraints. Show saved locally, syncing, synced and conflict states distinctly. Bound batches, compress deltas, back off retries and use Wi-Fi or charging policies for large attachments. Measure freshness without spending the battery on empty polls.

steps.q: A sleeping phone receives delayed push notifications. What promise can the sync protocol support?
choices: Subsecond background sync once the push provider accepts the notification
Confirmed delivery once the server persists its push outbox entry
Fast foreground sync and eventual background catch-up when the app runs
steps.why: Provider acceptance and durable intent are useful boundaries, but neither proves the phone has run or pulled changes.

steps.q: Can we delete tombstones after a week to cut storage? Follow-up: a laptop returns after a month.
checklist: Compare one-week tombstones with the supported month offline
Reject expired epochs or unknown bases before applying old uploads
Preserve unsynced edits while fetching and rebasing a fresh snapshot
steps.model: Only if our supported offline window and all recovery paths fit that week, or old clients are forced through a safe rebase. A month-old laptop cannot upload its old snapshot as truth. I would fetch a fresh snapshot, preserve its unsynced operations separately, validate base versions and surface conflicts. The extra deletion metadata buys a concrete promise about which disconnected clients can return safely.

steps.q: A device returns after its cursor and deletion history expired. How can it resume without reviving deleted notes?
choices: Fetch a snapshot, preserve queued edits and validate their old bases or surface conflicts
Fetch a snapshot, then overwrite it with all queued note bodies
Set the cursor to the current log head and upload rows missing from the snapshot
steps.why: A missing row could be a deletion. Old queued work needs version validation or user resolution, not unconditional replay.

takeaway: Save intent locally, resume with stable ids and cursors, and keep enough history to merge safely.
